chapters.n: Omni, Jarom’s son, writes a little as commanded so the family genealogy is preserved. The book of Omni contains five writers spanning more than two centuries.
Omni spent his days fighting to protect the Nephites from the Lamanites. He candidly admits he is “a wicked man” who did not keep God’s commandments as he should—a rare, honest confession.

f.w: I of myself am a wicked man
f.g: An unusually frank self-assessment from a record keeper.

chapters.n: Seasons of peace and war passed. After 282 years from Lehi’s departure (about 318 BC), Omni gave the plates to his son Amaron.

f.w: two hundred and eighty and two years

chapters.n: Amaron adds a few words in “the book of my father.”
By 320 years after Lehi (around 280 BC), the more wicked Nephites had been destroyed.
God fulfilled his warning: those who don’t keep his commandments won’t prosper in the land. The promise works both ways.

f.w: ye shall not prosper in the land

chapters.n: God sent severe judgment but spared and rescued the righteous.
Amaron passes the plates to his brother Chemish.
Chemish writes the shortest entry of any record keeper—one verse—noting he saw his brother write his final words the day he received the plates. They kept records as commanded.

f.w: according to the commandments of our fathers

chapters.n: Abinadom, Chemish’s son, saw much war and personally killed many Lamanites defending his people.
The kings kept the detailed record. Abinadom knows of no new revelation or prophecy beyond what’s already written. Spiritual life seems to have dimmed in this period.

f.w: plates which is had by the kings

chapters.n: Amaleki, Abinadom’s son, tells of Mosiah (the first), whom the Lord warned to flee the land of Nephi with all who would follow God’s voice.

f.g: Mosiah I, father of King Benjamin and grandfather of Mosiah II.

chapters.n: Mosiah obeyed. The faithful followed him into the wilderness, guided by preaching and prophecy, until they reached Zarahemla.

f.w: led by the power of his arm

chapters.n: There they found the people of Zarahemla, who rejoiced because Mosiah brought the brass plates containing the record of the Jews.
These people had left Jerusalem when King Zedekiah of Judah was taken to Babylon (about 587 BC). They are known as Mulekites, after Mulek, a surviving son of Zedekiah.
The Lord brought them across the ocean to this land, where they had lived ever since.

They had grown numerous but had suffered wars. Without written records, their language had become corrupted and they had lost faith in God. Mosiah’s people couldn’t understand them. Records preserve language and faith.
Mosiah taught them his language. Their leader Zarahemla then recited his genealogy from memory; it was written on other plates.

f.g: An oral genealogy, written down by Mosiah’s scribes.

chapters.n: The two peoples united and appointed Mosiah king.
A large engraved stone was brought to Mosiah, and he translated it “by the gift and power of God.”
The stone told of Coriantumr and his slain people. Coriantumr had been found by the people of Zarahemla and lived with them nine months.

It also told of his ancestors, who came from the tower when God confounded languages. They were destroyed by God’s just judgments, their bones scattered in the north. These are the Jaredites of the book of Ether.
Amaleki was born during Mosiah’s reign and lived to see his death. Mosiah’s son Benjamin became king.
Under King Benjamin there was a serious war, but the Nephites prevailed and drove the Lamanites from Zarahemla.

Old and childless, Amaleki gives the plates to righteous King Benjamin. He urges all to believe in prophecy, revelation, angels, tongues, and every good gift—for all good comes from God and evil from the devil.

f.w: there is nothing which is good save it comes from the Lord

chapters.n: A treasured invitation: come to Christ, the Holy One of Israel; offer him your “whole souls”; keep fasting and praying; endure to the end, and you will be saved.

f.w: offer your whole souls as an offering

chapters.n: Amaleki also tells of a group who wanted to return and reclaim their homeland, the land of Nephi.
Their strong but stubborn leader caused infighting; all but fifty were killed, and the survivors returned to Zarahemla.
Another, larger group set out again—led by Zeniff, whose story is told in Mosiah 9–22.
Amaleki’s brother went with them, and he never learned their fate. The plates are full, and Amaleki, near death, ends. The small plates end here.
